Question_text: A student investigates the oscillations of a metre rule. The student starts by supporting one end of a heavy rod using a stand, boss and clamp. Fig. 1.1 shows how he assembled the apparatus. Two clamps are used to support the rod horizontally, about 60 cm above the bench, as shown in Fig. 1.2. The student suspends the metre rule from the rod using two pieces of thread of equal length. A half-metre rule is placed on the bench, under the metre rule, so that the end A of the metre rule is above the 0cm end of the half-metre rule, as shown in Fig. 1.3. The student is given one square piece of card of side l. He attaches the centre of the card to the end A of the metre rule with a small piece of Blu-tack, as shown in Fig. 1.4. The value of l is 19.0 cm. The student repeats the experiment in (c) to obtain a value for Nav. He then cuts the card to make the square smaller and repeats the experiment with smaller values of l. Fig. 1.5 shows the student's results. On Fig. 1.6, plot the graph of l/cm on the y-axis against Nav on the x-axis. Start your axes from (0,0). Draw the smooth curve of best fit.
image: Fig. 1.1 shows a diagram of a heavy rod supported horizontally by a clamp, which is attached to a boss, which in turn is attached to a stand. The stand rests on a bench. The clamp and boss are positioned high on the stand, with the rod extending to the right. The labels are 'boss', 'clamp', 'rod', 'stand', 'bench'. Fig. 1.2 shows a diagram of a horizontal rod supported by two clamps. Each clamp is attached to a stand (not fully shown, just the boss and clamp structure). The rod is labeled 'rod', and the clamps are labeled 'clamp'. An 'X' is marked on the rod near both clamps, indicating points to be checked. The base is labeled 'bench'. Fig. 1.3 shows a diagram of a metre rule suspended horizontally by two pieces of thread of equal length. The threads are attached to a rod, which is held by two clamps. Below the suspended metre rule, a half-metre rule is placed on the bench. The end 'A' of the metre rule is aligned vertically above the '0 cm' mark of the half-metre rule. Marks for '10 cm' and '5 cm' are also visible on the half-metre rule. Labels include 'clamp', 'rod', 'thread', 'metre rule', 'A', 'half-metre rule', 'bench', '10 cm', '5 cm'. Fig. 1.4 shows a diagram of a square piece of card attached to the end 'A' of a metre rule using Blu-tack. The side length of the card is labeled 'l'. The metre rule is shown extending to the left. Fig. 1.5 shows a table presenting experimental results with two columns: 'l/cm' and 'Nav'. The data includes rows for (19.0, 3), (15.0, 6), (11.0, 12), (7.0, 22), (3.0, 35), and (0, blank). Fig. 1.6 shows a blank graph grid with horizontal (x) and vertical (y) axes starting from the origin (0,0). The grid is divided into major and minor squares, suitable for plotting data.

Parts.part_text: Explain why this is not the best way to assemble one stand, boss and clamp to support a heavy rod.
In the space to the right of Fig. 1.1, sketch a better way of assembling this apparatus.
The student is given a metre rule and two set-squares to check that the rod is horizontal. Draw on Fig. 1.2 to show how the apparatus is used.
Explain how he can tell that the rod is horizontal.
Describe how the student can check that the end A of the metre rule is exactly above the 0 cm end of the half-metre rule.

The metre rule is moved to the left until the end A is above the 10cm mark on the half-metre rule. It is then released. As the metre rule swings, the amplitude of the swing decreases. The student counts the number N of swings until end A no longer passes the 5cm mark on the half-metre rule. He repeats this several times and his results are shown below. 53, 55, 52, 51, 53. Calculate Nav, the average value of N. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
Complete Fig. 1.5 by recording your value for Nav from (c)(ii) for l = 0.
On Fig. 1.6, plot the graph of l/cm on the y-axis against Nav on the x-axis. Start your axes from (0,0). Draw the smooth curve of best fit.

The graph shows that as l decreases, Nav increases. Two quantities x and y are inversely proportional if they obey the equation x = k/y where k is a constant. By taking two pairs of values from the graph, show that Nav is not inversely proportional to l.
Suggest why the student starts with l = 19cm and then reduces l, rather than starts with l = 3 cm and then increases l.

Question_text: A student investigates the path of a ray of light through a triangular prism. Fig. 2.1 on page 7 shows the triangular prism placed in the centre of a sheet of white paper. Fig. 2.2 shows a ray box that produces a narrow ray of light.
image: Fig. 2.1 shows a drawing of a triangular prism, with vertices labeled A, B, C, placed in the center of a sheet of white paper. The prism is oriented such that side AB is at the bottom left, BC is the right side, and AC is the top side. The overall sheet is labeled 'white paper' and the prism 'triangular prism'. Fig. 2.2 shows a diagram of a ray box, a rectangular device with an 'electric lead' connected to it. It has an opening from which a 'narrow ray of light' is emitted.

Parts.part_text: On Fig. 2.1, mark and label P, the mid-point of the side AB of the prism,
draw the normal to the prism at P,
draw a line to represent a ray of light incident at P with an angle of incidence of 40°.
Describe how the student can use the narrow ray of light to find the path of the ray through the prism.

Question_text: A group of students measures forces using a set of bathroom scales. One student measures his weight by standing on the scales, as shown in Fig. 3.1. Fig. 3.2 shows the reading on the scales when the student is standing still. Two students use the scales to measure the maximum friction force between a bench and a heavy box. One student places the scales against the side of the box, as shown in Fig. 3.3. He pushes the scales with both hands and the other student notes the reading on the scales when the box just starts to move.

Fig. 3.3 shows a diagram of bathroom scales positioned against the side of a 'box' which is resting on a 'bench'. An arrow indicates a horizontal pushing force applied to the scales.

Question_text: Fig. 4.1 shows an empty large reel that was used to hold ribbon. The central cylinder has a diameter of about 3 cm. Two students use different methods to find the diameter of the central cylinder. One student uses a ruler and the apparatus shown in Fig. 4.2 when finding the diameter. The distance between points A and B changes as the screw is turned.
image: Fig. 4.1 shows a diagram of an empty large reel, typically used for holding ribbon. It consists of two circular flanges and a central cylindrical core. The components are labeled 'reel' and 'central cylinder'. Fig. 4.2 shows a diagram of a type of caliper or screw gauge apparatus. It has two jaws, one fixed and one movable by a 'screw'. The points of measurement are labeled 'A' and 'B'. This device is used for measuring the diameter of objects.

Parts.part_text: Describe how the student measures the diameter.

The other student measures the diameter using only the following apparatus: metre rule, pencil, Blu-tack, one metre of thin thread. Describe clearly how she can find an accurate value for the diameter.
